{{Short description|Type of Horn clause, a generalization of identities}}
{{Multiple issues|
{{one source |date=May 2024}}

In [[universal algebra]], a '''quasi-identity''' is an implication of the form

:''s''<sub>1</sub> = ''t''<sub>1</sub> ∧ … ∧ ''s''<sub>''n''</sub> = ''t''<sub>''n''</sub> → ''s'' = ''t''

where ''s''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''s''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''t''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''t''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''s'', and ''t'' are [[term (logic)|terms]] built up from variables using the operation symbols of the specified [[signature (logic)|signature]].

A quasi-identity amounts to a conditional equation for which the conditions themselves are equations. Alternatively, it can be seen as a disjunction of inequations and one equation ''s''<sub>1</sub> ≠ ''t''<sub>1</sub> ∨ ... ∨ ''s''<sub>''n''</sub> ≠ ''t''<sub>''n''</sub> ∨ ''s'' = ''t''—that is, as a definite [[Horn clause]]. A quasi-identity with ''n'' = 0 is an ordinary [[Identity (mathematics)|identity]] or equation, so quasi-identities are a generalization of identities.
